topics.title: Earth and space
topics.intro: Why do we have day and night? Why are there seasons? Let’s find out what you think first.
topics.teach: Explain why we have day and night.
topics.talk: Ask her why it is dark at night, then why it is colder in winter.
topics.hook: Spin gives a **day**, orbit gives a **year**, tilt gives the **seasons**.

topics.title: Forces
topics.intro: Forces are pushes and pulls. Some ideas about forces feel right but are wrong. Let’s test yours.
topics.teach: Explain what would happen if you dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon.
topics.talk: Ask her why a ball rolling on grass slows down.
topics.hook: Forces are pushes and pulls, measured in **newtons**: they change an object’s speed, direction or shape.

topics.title: Light and seeing
topics.intro: How do we see things? The answer surprised scientists for centuries.
topics.teach: Explain how you see a book on a table.
topics.talk: Ask her why a shadow forms.
topics.hook: **Source → Object → Eye**, and always in straight lines.

topics.title: Electrical circuits
topics.intro: Circuits need a complete loop. Let’s check what you know about how they work.
topics.teach: Explain why a bulb doesn’t light if the circuit has a gap.
topics.talk: Ask her what a switch actually does inside a circuit.
topics.hook: **No loop, no flow**: a circuit must be complete, with no gaps.

topics.title: Materials and changes
topics.intro: When sugar dissolves, where does it go? When we bake a cake, can we undo it? Let’s see.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between a reversible and an irreversible change.
topics.talk: Ask her how she would get salt back out of salty water.
topics.hook: Can you undo it? Melting, freezing, dissolving: **reversible**. Burning, rusting, baking: **irreversible**.

topics.title: Classifying living things
topics.intro: Scientists sort living things into groups by their features.
topics.teach: Explain how you could tell a mammal from a reptile.
topics.talk: Ask her whether a whale is a fish or a mammal, and why.
topics.hook: **K**ing **P**hilip **C**ame **O**ver **F**or **G**ood **S**oup: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

head: group
key features
example
rows: live in water; gills, scales and fins
moist skin; young live in water (gills), adults on land (lungs)
dry, scaly skin; most lay eggs on land
feathers and a beak; lay hard-shelled eggs
hair or fur; breathe air; feed their babies milk
visual.caption: The five vertebrate groups. A whale lives in water, but it breathes air and feeds its babies milk: it is a mammal.

topics.title: The heart, blood and health
topics.intro: Your heart beats about 100 000 times a day. What is it actually doing?
topics.teach: Explain the journey of blood from the heart to the lungs and back.
topics.talk: Ask her to take her pulse before and after running on the spot.
topics.hook: **A**rteries carry blood **A**way from the heart; v**ein**s bring it back **in**.

topics.title: Evolution and inheritance
topics.intro: How did giraffes get long necks? Darwin had an answer that changed science.
topics.teach: Explain how natural selection works using the giraffe.
topics.talk: Ask her what Mary Anning discovered.
topics.hook: “Survival of the fittest”: the best-suited survive, breed and pass on their features.

steps: Giraffes vary: some have longer necks
Those giraffes survive and breed more
Over many generations, necks get longer
visual.caption: Natural selection: nobody stretches their neck. The giraffes that happen to suit their habitat best survive and pass their features on.

items.prompt: Why do we have day and night?

options.text: The Earth spins on its axis
The Sun moves around the Earth
options.feedback: The Sun appears to move, but it is the Earth that turns.

options.text: The Earth orbits the Sun once a day
options.feedback: One orbit of the Sun takes a year, not a day.

options.text: The Moon blocks out the Sun at night
options.feedback: The Moon is often visible during the day, and it doesn’t cause night.

items.explain: As the Earth spins, your side faces towards the Sun (day) then away from it (night).
items.hook: The Earth spins like a roast on a spit: whichever side faces the Sun has day.
items.example: The Sun seems to cross the sky from east to west each day, but really you are being carried round by the spinning Earth.

items.prompt: Why is it colder in the UK in winter?

options.text: Our half of the tilted Earth leans away from the Sun
The Earth is further from the Sun in winter
options.feedback: Surprisingly, the Earth is closest to the Sun in early January! Seasons are caused by the tilt.

options.text: The Sun gives out less heat during winter
options.feedback: The Sun’s output doesn’t change with our seasons.

items.explain: The Earth’s axis is tilted by about 23.5°. When the Northern Hemisphere leans away from the Sun, sunlight is spread out and days are short: winter.
items.hook: **Tilt, not distance**: the Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January.
items.example: Shine a torch straight down and you get a small bright spot; tilt it and the light spreads out and is weaker. That is UK winter sunlight.

items.prompt: Why does the Moon seem to change shape over a month?

options.text: We see different amounts of its lit half
The Earth’s shadow covers part of it
options.feedback: The Earth’s shadow only falls on the Moon during an eclipse, which is rare.

options.text: Clouds in space cover part of it
options.feedback: The phases happen even on clear nights.

items.explain: Half the Moon is always lit by the Sun. As it orbits us (about 29.5 days), we see more or less of the lit half.
items.hook: **DOC**: in the UK the Moon grows from a D shape to an O (full), then shrinks to a C shape.
items.example: Look at the Moon from your window on clear evenings a week apart and watch the lit part grow or shrink.

items.prompt: How long does the Earth take to orbit the Sun?
items.explain: One orbit takes about 365¼ days. The extra quarter-days add up to a leap day every 4 years.
items.hook: 365 days in a year, 366 in a **leap year**: the four leftover quarter-days make one extra day.
items.example: 2024 was a leap year with a 29 February; the next one is 2028.

items.prompt: Roughly how long does the Moon take to orbit the Earth?
items.explain: The Moon orbits the Earth in about 27 days; the cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days.
items.hook: **Moon** and **month** come from the same old word: one trip of the Moon is about a month.
items.example: A full Moon comes round about once a month: many calendars and diaries show the Moon’s phases.

items.prompt: What kind of object is the Sun?
items.explain: The Sun is a star: a huge ball of hot gas. It is the closest star to Earth.
items.hook: Stars make their own light; planets and moons only reflect it. The Sun shines, so it’s a star.
items.example: Each twinkling star you see on a clear night is a sun, many of them bigger than ours, just very far away.

items.prompt: Put the planets in order from the Sun, starting with the closest.
items.explain: My Very Easy Method Just Speeds Up Naming: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
items.hook: **M**y **V**ery **E**asy **M**ethod **J**ust **S**peeds **U**p **N**aming.
items.example: The brightest “star” low in the west just after sunset is often not a star at all, but the planet Venus.

items.prompt: Which is the largest planet in our solar system?
items.explain: Jupiter is so big that more than 1000 Earths could fit inside it.
items.hook: **J**upiter is the **J**umbo planet.
items.example: If the Earth were a pea, Jupiter would be about the size of a tennis ball.

items.prompt: What shape are the Sun, Earth and Moon?
items.explain: They are all roughly spheres, pulled into ball shapes by gravity.
items.hook: Gravity pulls everything towards the middle equally, squeezing huge objects into balls.
items.example: Photos taken from the International Space Station show the Earth’s curved edge.

items.prompt: Who argued, in the 1500s, that the Earth orbits the Sun?
items.explain: Nicolaus Copernicus proposed a Sun-centred (heliocentric) model. Galileo later found evidence for it.
items.hook: **Co**pernicus put the Sun at the **co**re of the solar system.
items.example: Helio- means Sun: the gas helium was named because it was first discovered in the Sun’s light.

items.prompt: A hammer and a feather are dropped together on the Moon, where there is no air. What happens?

options.text: They hit the ground at the same time
The hammer lands first because it is heavier
options.feedback: On Earth air resistance slows the feather. With no air, gravity speeds up all objects at the same rate. An astronaut tested this on the Moon in 1971!

options.text: The feather floats away
options.feedback: The Moon has gravity, so the feather falls too.

items.explain: Without air resistance, all objects fall with the same acceleration, whatever their mass.
items.hook: No air, no difference: gravity speeds everything up at the same rate.
items.example: On the Apollo 15 mission in 1971, astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon. They landed together.

items.prompt: A ball is rolling across a flat, grassy field. Why does it slow down and stop?

options.text: Friction from the grass
It runs out of the force from the kick
options.feedback: Objects don’t carry a store of “force”. A moving object keeps moving unless a force (here friction) acts on it.

options.text: Gravity pulls it backwards
options.feedback: Gravity pulls down, not backwards.

items.explain: Friction acts in the opposite direction to the motion and slows the ball. On ice, with less friction, it would roll much further.
items.hook: Moving things keep moving unless a force acts: friction is the thief that steals speed.
items.example: A ball rolls much further across a smooth playground or an ice rink than across long grass.

items.prompt: What is the difference between mass and weight?

options.text: Mass is matter (kg); weight is gravity’s pull (N)
They are the same thing, measured in kilograms
options.feedback: In everyday speech we mix them up, but in science weight is a force measured in newtons.

options.text: Weight is measured in kg; mass in newtons
options.feedback: It is the other way round: mass in kg, weight in newtons (N).

items.explain: Your mass is the same on the Moon, but your weight is about one-sixth because the Moon’s gravity is weaker.
items.hook: **M**ass is the **M**atter in you (kg); **W**eight is the **W**orld’s pull on you (N).
items.example: Bathroom scales show kg but really measure your weight: on the Moon they would read about one-sixth as much.

items.prompt: What unit are forces measured in?
items.explain: Forces are measured in newtons (N), after Isaac Newton.
items.hook: **N** for **N**ewton: forces are measured in newtons (N).
items.example: An apple weighs about 1 newton, fitting for the scientist in the falling-apple story!

items.prompt: Which force slows down a parachutist?
items.explain: The large parachute pushes against lots of air, increasing air resistance.
items.hook: Bigger surface, more air to push aside, more air resistance.
items.example: Drop a flat sheet of paper and it drifts down; scrunch the same sheet into a ball and it falls fast.

items.prompt: Why are boats and fish streamlined?
items.explain: A streamlined shape lets water flow past easily, so less force is wasted.
items.hook: Streamlined = smooth and pointed, so water slips past instead of pushing back.
items.example: Swimmers push off the pool wall with their arms stretched into a point to cut through the water.

items.prompt: Which simple machine is a see-saw an example of?
items.explain: A lever turns around a pivot. A small force far from the pivot can lift a big load.
items.hook: Archimedes is said to have boasted: “Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth” (with a long enough lever).
items.example: Scissors, a crowbar and a bottle opener are all levers turning on a pivot.

items.prompt: What simple machine uses a rope over a wheel to lift loads more easily?
items.explain: A single pulley changes the direction of your pull; several pulleys together let a smaller force lift a heavy load by pulling over a longer distance.
items.hook: A pulley turns your pull **down** into a lift **up**.
items.example: Pull a flagpole’s rope down and the flag goes up, thanks to a pulley at the top.

items.prompt: What are wheels with teeth that turn each other called?
items.explain: Gears change the speed or direction of turning, as in a bicycle.
items.hook: Gears are toothed wheels that bite into each other, so turning one turns the next.
items.example: Changing to a low gear on a bike makes pedalling uphill easier.

items.prompt: Which scientist described the law of gravity in 1687?
items.explain: Newton explained that every object pulls on every other object; Earth’s pull on us is our weight.
items.hook: The famous story: an apple falling from a tree set Newton thinking about gravity.
items.example: Newton’s childhood home, Woolsthorpe Manor in Lincolnshire, still has the apple tree linked to the story.

items.prompt: How do we see a book on a table?

options.text: Light from a source bounces off the book and travels into our eyes
Light travels out of our eyes to the book
options.feedback: Ancient Greeks thought this, but our eyes only receive light. In a dark room you can’t see at all.

options.text: Our eyes see it because it is there, light isn’t needed
options.feedback: Without light we can’t see anything.

items.explain: We see objects when light reflects off them and enters our eyes. Light sources (like the Sun or a lamp) give out their own light.
items.hook: **Source → Object → Eye**: light travels into your eyes, never out of them.
items.example: In a room with no windows and the light off, you can’t see a thing, because no light is bouncing into your eyes.

items.prompt: Why does a shadow have the same shape as the object?

options.text: Light travels in straight lines
The shadow is a reflection of the object
options.feedback: A reflection shows colour and detail; a shadow is just where light is blocked.

options.text: Darkness comes out of the object
options.feedback: Darkness isn’t a thing that moves. A shadow is simply an absence of light.

items.explain: Because light travels in straight lines, an opaque object blocks it, leaving a dark area shaped like the object.
items.hook: A shadow is an object-shaped gap in the light, where straight-line light is blocked.
items.example: Make shadow-puppet animals with your hands in front of a torch shining on a wall.

items.prompt: Light travels in…
items.explain: Light travels in straight lines (until it hits something and reflects or refracts).
items.hook: Light can’t turn corners: you can hear someone round a corner, but you can’t see them.
items.example: Sunbeams through a gap in the curtains, or through clouds, make straight lines like a ruler.

items.prompt: What is a material that lets no light through called?
items.explain: Opaque materials (wood, metal) block light. Transparent ones (clear glass) let it through. Translucent ones (frosted glass) let some through.
items.hook: **O**paque: “**O**h no, nothing gets through!”
items.example: Blackout curtains are opaque, which is why they keep a bedroom dark on light summer evenings.

items.prompt: What is a material that lets some light through, but you can’t see clearly through it, called?
items.explain: Tracing paper and frosted glass are translucent.
items.hook: Transparent = see-through. Translucent = light gets through, but the view is blurry.
items.example: A frosted bathroom window lets light in but stops people seeing in.

items.prompt: What happens to light when it hits a mirror?
items.explain: Smooth, shiny surfaces like mirrors reflect light in a regular way, so we see an image.
items.hook: Mirrors bounce light back, like a ball bouncing off a wall.
items.example: Ambulances have AMBULANCE written back-to-front on the bonnet so drivers ahead can read it in their mirrors.

items.prompt: Which device uses two mirrors so you can see over a wall?
items.explain: A periscope has two mirrors at 45° that reflect light round a corner.
items.hook: **Peri-** means “around”: a periscope lets you look around things.
items.example: Submarines use periscopes to see above the waves while staying hidden underwater.

items.prompt: Which of these is a light source?
items.explain: The Moon only reflects sunlight; it is not a light source.
items.hook: Makes its own light? Source. Only bounces light? Reflector, like the Moon.
items.example: Cat’s eyes on UK roads shine in headlights, but they are reflectors, not light sources.

items.prompt: In a simple circuit with a bulb, what happens to the electric current?

options.text: It flows all the way round the circuit and is not used up
It is used up by the bulb, so less comes back to the cell
options.feedback: A very common idea! The current is the same all the way round. It is energy that is transferred to the bulb, not current.

options.text: It only flows from the cell to the bulb
options.feedback: Current needs a complete loop and flows all the way round.

items.explain: Current is the flow of charge round the circuit. The cell pushes it; the bulb transfers energy as light and heat.
items.hook: Current is like a bike chain: it moves all the way round, and none of it gets used up.

items.prompt: You add a second cell (battery) in series to a circuit with one bulb. What happens?

options.text: The bulb gets brighter
The bulb gets dimmer
options.feedback: More cells push harder, so more current flows and the bulb is brighter.

options.text: Nothing changes
options.feedback: The voltage increases, so the bulb changes.

items.explain: More cells means a higher voltage, which pushes more current through the bulb, making it brighter. Adding more bulbs instead would make each one dimmer.
items.hook: More cells = more push = brighter bulb. More bulbs = push shared = dimmer bulbs.
items.example: Torches often hold two or three cells in a row (in series) to give the bulb a bigger push.

items.prompt: What does a circuit need for current to flow?
items.answer: a complete loop with no gaps
items.explain: Any gap breaks the circuit and the current stops.
items.hook: No loop, no flow!
items.example: A broken wire inside a headphone cable leaves a gap, so the sound cuts out.

items.prompt: What does a switch do in a circuit?
items.answer: it opens or closes a gap in the circuit
items.explain: An open switch makes a gap; a closed switch completes the loop.
items.hook: Switch **C**losed = circuit **C**omplete = on.
items.example: Pressing a light switch at home closes or opens a gap in the circuit to the light.

items.prompt: What is a material that lets electricity flow through it called?
items.explain: Metals like copper are good conductors. Plastic and rubber are insulators.
items.hook: Metals conduct; plastic, rubber, wood and glass insulate.
items.example: A UK plug has brass (metal) pins to conduct and a plastic case to insulate.

items.prompt: Why are wires covered in plastic?
distractors: plastic makes the current flow faster
only to make the wires bendy
items.explain: The plastic coating stops current flowing into us.
items.hook: An insulator is a coat for the wire: it keeps the current in, like a coat keeps heat in.
items.example: Look at a phone charger cable: copper wire inside, a plastic or rubber coating outside.

items.prompt: In a circuit diagram, a circle with a cross inside is the symbol for…
items.explain: Bulb: circle with a cross. Cell: a long and a short line. Motor: circle with an M.
items.hook: The cross in the bulb symbol is like the glowing wire inside a glass bulb.

items.prompt: What unit measures how hard a cell pushes the current?
items.explain: Voltage is measured in volts (V). A typical AA cell is 1.5 V.
items.hook: **V**olts measure **V**oltage: the push.
items.example: AA and AAA batteries are printed with 1.5 V; a square smoke-alarm battery says 9 V.

items.prompt: You dissolve 10 g of sugar in 100 g of water. What is the mass of the sugary water?

options.text: 100 g, because the sugar disappears
options.feedback: The sugar breaks into particles too small to see, but they are still there, and so is their mass.

options.text: Less than 100 g
options.feedback: Nothing is lost: mass is conserved.

items.explain: When something dissolves, its particles spread out between the water particles. The total mass stays the same: 110 g.
items.hook: Dissolved isn’t disappeared: mass in = mass out.
items.example: Stir sugar into tea: you can’t see it, but you can still taste it, so it must still be there.

items.prompt: Which of these is an irreversible change?

options.text: Burning paper
Melting ice
options.feedback: Melted ice can be frozen again, so this is reversible.

options.text: Dissolving salt in water
options.feedback: You can get the salt back by evaporating the water, so this is reversible.

options.text: Freezing orange juice
options.feedback: It can melt back, so it is reversible.

items.explain: Burning makes new materials (ash, smoke and gases). You can’t turn them back into paper.
items.hook: Ask: can I get it back? If not, it’s irreversible. You can’t unbake a cake.
items.example: Toast can’t be turned back into bread, but a melted ice lolly can be refrozen.

items.prompt: Puddles disappear on a sunny day. Where does the water go?

options.text: It evaporates into the air
It all soaks down into the ground
options.feedback: Some does, but puddles on a playground disappear because the water evaporates.

options.text: The Sun’s heat destroys the water
options.feedback: Matter isn’t destroyed. The water is still there as a gas.

items.explain: Heat from the Sun gives water particles energy to escape as water vapour (a gas).
items.hook: Evaporation: water particles escape into the air as invisible water vapour.
items.example: Wet washing on a line dries fastest on a warm, windy day.

items.prompt: How could you separate sand from water?
items.explain: Sand doesn’t dissolve, so a filter paper traps it and lets water through.
items.hook: A filter is a super-fine sieve: it catches bits that haven’t dissolved.
items.example: A tea bag or a coffee filter lets water through but traps the leaves or grounds.

items.prompt: How could you get salt back from salty water?
items.explain: Salt dissolves, so filtering won’t work. Heating evaporates the water and leaves the salt behind.
items.hook: Salt hides in water, but stays behind when the water evaporates.
items.example: White marks on wellies after a day at the seaside are salt left behind as the seawater dried.

items.prompt: How could you separate iron filings from sand?
items.explain: Iron is magnetic; sand is not.
items.hook: Magnets pick out iron (and nickel and cobalt), not sand and not most other metals.
items.example: Recycling centres use giant magnets to pull steel cans out from aluminium ones.

items.prompt: A substance that dissolves in water is called…
items.explain: Sugar and salt are soluble. Sand and chalk are insoluble.
items.hook: **Sol**uble things dis**sol**ve.
items.example: Sugar disappears into tea; sand stays gritty at the bottom of a bucket of water.

items.prompt: What are the three states of matter?
items.explain: Matter exists as solids, liquids and gases. Ice, water and steam are the three states of one substance.
items.hook: Solid keeps its shape, liquid takes the shape, gas fills the space.
items.example: An ice cube melts into a puddle, and the puddle slowly dries up: one substance, all three states.

items.prompt: At what temperature does pure water boil (at sea level)?
items.explain: Water boils at 100°C and freezes at 0°C.
items.hook: Water freezes at **0** and boils at **100**: the Celsius scale was built around it.
items.example: A kettle clicks off when its water reaches boiling point, about 100°C.

items.prompt: What is the irreversible change when iron reacts with water and oxygen?
items.explain: Rust (iron oxide) is a new material, so rusting is irreversible.
items.hook: Rust needs **water and oxygen** together: take either away and iron won’t rust.
items.example: A bike left out in the rain gets an orange, rusty chain.

items.prompt: Is a whale a fish or a mammal?

options.text: A mammal: it breathes air and feeds milk
A fish: it lives in water and has fins
options.feedback: Living in water doesn’t make an animal a fish. Whales breathe air and feed their babies milk.

options.text: Neither: it is a type of reptile
options.feedback: Reptiles have scales and most lay eggs on land.

items.explain: Classification is based on features, not habitat. Whales are mammals.
items.hook: Breathes air and feeds its baby milk? Mammal, wherever it lives.
items.example: Dolphins and grey seals around UK coasts are mammals too: watch them come up to breathe.

head: group
key features
example
rows: live in water; gills, scales and fins
moist skin; young live in water (gills), adults on land (lungs)
dry, scaly skin; most lay eggs on land
feathers and a beak; lay hard-shelled eggs
hair or fur; breathe air; feed their babies milk
visual.caption: The five vertebrate groups. A whale lives in water, but it breathes air and feeds its babies milk: it is a mammal.

items.prompt: What is an animal with a backbone called?
items.explain: Vertebrates have backbones: fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
items.hook: **Vertebr**ate = has **vertebr**ae, the bones of a backbone.
items.example: Run a finger down the middle of your back: those bumps are your vertebrae.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the five vertebrate groups?
items.explain: The five vertebrate groups are fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. Insects are invertebrates.
items.hook: **MR FAB**: **M**ammals, **R**eptiles, **F**ish, **A**mphibians, **B**irds.
items.example: A garden can hold all five: a hedgehog, a slow-worm, goldfish in the pond, a frog and a robin.

head: group
key features
example
rows: live in water; gills, scales and fins
moist skin; young live in water (gills), adults on land (lungs)
dry, scaly skin; most lay eggs on land
feathers and a beak; lay hard-shelled eggs
hair or fur; breathe air; feed their babies milk
visual.caption: The five vertebrate groups. A whale lives in water, but it breathes air and feeds its babies milk: it is a mammal.

items.prompt: Which group do frogs belong to?
items.explain: Amphibians usually start life in water (with gills) and live on land as adults (with lungs).
items.hook: **Amphibian** means “double life”: in water as a tadpole, on land as an adult.
items.example: Frogspawn in a pond in spring hatches into tadpoles, which grow legs and become froglets.

items.prompt: How many legs does an insect have?
items.explain: Insects have six legs and three body parts. Spiders, with eight legs, are arachnids, not insects.
items.hook: Six legs and three body parts (head, thorax, abdomen) = insect. Eight legs = spider.
items.example: Count the legs on a ladybird (6) and a garden spider (8) next time you find one.

items.prompt: Which scientist invented the two-part naming system for living things (like Homo sapiens)?
items.explain: Carl Linnaeus, an 18th-century Swedish scientist, gave every species a genus and species name.
items.hook: Linnaeus gave each species a two-part name, like a surname then a first name: Genus, then species.
items.example: A pet cat is Felis catus; a robin is Erithacus rubecula.

items.prompt: Living things too small to see without a microscope are called…
items.explain: Micro-organisms include bacteria and some fungi. Some cause disease; others help us make bread and yoghurt.
items.hook: **Micro** means tiny, as in microscope: micro-organisms are tiny living things.
items.example: Yeast makes bread dough rise, and bacteria turn milk into yoghurt: both are micro-organisms.

items.prompt: What is a tool of yes/no questions used to identify living things called?
items.explain: A classification (branching) key sorts organisms using questions about their features.
items.hook: A key works like the game 20 Questions: each yes/no answer narrows it down.
items.example: Spotter guides to British minibeasts or wild flowers often use keys.

items.prompt: What does the heart do?

options.text: It pumps blood around the body
It makes new blood for the body
options.feedback: Blood cells are made in the bone marrow, not the heart.

options.text: It cleans the blood of waste
options.feedback: Cleaning waste out of the blood is mainly the job of the kidneys (and the liver), not the heart.

items.explain: The heart is a muscle that pumps blood, carrying oxygen and nutrients to every part of the body.
items.hook: The heart is a pump, not a factory or a filter: blood is made in bone marrow.
items.example: Squeeze a squeezy bottle of water to feel how a pump pushes liquid out.

items.prompt: Why does your heart beat faster when you exercise?

options.text: Your muscles need more oxygen
The heart gets nervous and scared
options.feedback: The heart responds to what the muscles need.

options.text: Exercise makes your heart smaller
options.feedback: Exercise strengthens the heart over time; it doesn’t make it smaller.

items.explain: Working muscles need more oxygen and glucose, so the heart pumps faster and you breathe faster.
items.hook: Muscles shout “more oxygen!” and the heart answers by beating faster.
items.example: Feel your pulse after running up the stairs: it’s much faster than when you sit still.

items.prompt: Which blood vessels carry blood away from the heart?
items.explain: Arteries carry blood away from the heart (A for Away). Veins carry it back.
items.hook: **A**rteries carry blood **A**way from the heart.
items.example: When a nurse takes your pulse at your wrist, they’re feeling an artery.

items.prompt: Which blood vessels carry blood back to the heart?
items.explain: Veins carry blood back to the heart.
items.hook: Arteries go **A**way; v**ein**s bring blood back **in** to the heart.
items.example: The bluish lines on the inside of your wrist are veins.

items.prompt: What are the tiniest blood vessels, where oxygen passes into the cells, called?
items.explain: Capillaries are thinner than a hair, so substances can pass through their walls.
items.hook: **Capillary** comes from the Latin for “hair”: they are hair-thin.
items.example: When you graze your knee, the tiny beads of blood come from broken capillaries.

items.prompt: Where does blood pick up oxygen?
items.explain: In the lungs, oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out to be breathed away.
items.hook: Lungs are a swap shop: oxygen **in**, carbon dioxide **out**.
items.example: Breathe into a balloon: the air inside has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than room air.

items.prompt: Blood carries water, nutrients and oxygen. What else does it carry away from cells?
items.explain: Blood carries waste such as carbon dioxide away from cells.
items.hook: Blood is a delivery van: it drops off oxygen and food and picks up the rubbish.

items.prompt: What do you call the beat you can feel in your wrist or neck?
items.explain: Each pulse is one heartbeat pushing blood through an artery.
items.hook: Count your pulse for 15 seconds and multiply by 4 to get beats per minute.
items.example: A fitness watch or smartwatch measures your pulse (heart rate).

items.prompt: How did giraffes come to have long necks?

options.text: Longer-necked giraffes survived and passed it on
Each giraffe stretched its neck, and its babies inherited it
options.feedback: This was Lamarck’s idea, and it’s wrong: changes you make during your life aren’t passed to your children.

options.text: Giraffes decided that they needed longer necks
options.feedback: Animals can’t choose to evolve. Natural selection works on random differences.

items.explain: Natural selection: random variation, then the best-suited individuals survive and reproduce more, so the trait becomes common over many generations.
items.hook: “Survival of the fittest”: giraffes didn’t stretch; the longer-necked ones survived more.
items.example: Peppered moths: when soot blackened trees near Victorian factories, dark moths were better hidden and became common.

steps: Giraffes vary: some have longer necks
Those giraffes survive and breed more
Over many generations, necks get longer
visual.caption: Natural selection: nobody stretches their neck. The giraffes that happen to suit their habitat best survive and pass their features on.

items.prompt: Do offspring look exactly like their parents?

options.text: No: they inherit features from both parents, so they vary
Yes, always identical
options.feedback: Brothers and sisters look different, even with the same parents.

options.text: They only inherit features from their mother
options.feedback: Offspring inherit from both parents.

items.explain: Offspring inherit a mix of characteristics from their parents. This variation is what natural selection acts on.
items.hook: Half your genes from Mum, half from Dad, mixed differently each time, so siblings differ.
items.example: Brothers and sisters often share features, like hair colour, but rarely look identical (unless they are identical twins).

items.prompt: Which scientist explained evolution by natural selection in “On the Origin of Species” (1859)?
items.explain: Darwin developed his ideas after his voyage on HMS Beagle, including studying finches in the Galápagos Islands.
items.hook: **Darwin** sailed round the world on a ship called the **Beagle**.
items.example: Darwin was on the back of the Bank of England £10 note from 2000 to 2018.

items.prompt: Which fossil hunter from Lyme Regis discovered famous ichthyosaur and plesiosaur skeletons in the early 1800s?
items.explain: Mary Anning (1799–1847) made major fossil discoveries, though as a woman she was shut out of scientific societies.
items.hook: The tongue-twister “She sells seashells on the seashore” is said to be about Mary Anning.
items.example: You can still hunt for fossils on the beach at Lyme Regis, on Dorset’s Jurassic Coast.

items.prompt: What is a fossil?
items.answer: remains of an ancient living thing
distractors: a type of crystal found in caves
an animal still alive inside rock
a rock made by cooling lava
items.explain: Fossils form when remains are buried and slowly replaced by minerals. They show how living things have changed.
items.hook: Fossils are nature’s photos of the past, turned to stone.
items.example: The Natural History Museum in London displays fossils, including some found by Mary Anning.

items.prompt: A feature that helps a living thing survive in its habitat is called…
items.explain: A polar bear’s thick fur and a cactus’s spines are adaptations.
items.hook: Adaptations are survival tools: thick fur for cold, spines for protection, camouflage for hiding.
items.example: A hedgehog’s spines protect it from predators; a duck’s webbed feet help it swim.

items.prompt: On which islands did Darwin study finches with different beaks?
items.explain: The finches’ beaks suited the food on each island.
items.hook: The Galápagos are named after their giant tortoises: galápago is an old Spanish word for tortoise.
